title: Two tornadoes were confirmed from a rare storm that produced golf-ball size hailstones

Two tornadoes confirmed in the Philly region in rare November hail storm

 Hard freezes are expected in most of the region the next several mornings. 
 Hail descends on Gloucester City on Thursday on one of the region's wildest weather days on record. Read more Elizabeth Robertson / Staff Photographer by Anthony R. Wood Updated  Nov. 13, 2026, 4:56 p.m. ET | Published  Nov. 13, 2026, 12:35 p.m. ET Listen to article •   0:00 min While most of the region is likely to experience hard freezes for the next several mornings, after one of the more incredible weather events in the Philly region’s weather history, a few ice puddles aren’t likely to get much attention. 
 The National Weather Service confirmed that two rare November tornadoes touched down in the region on Thursday — one near Wilmington, and another in Chesterfield, Burlington County . 
 The latter, an EF1 on the Enhanced Fujita scale with top winds of 100 mph, traveled about 1.5 miles and damaged three buildings, a weather service team said. A report on the Delaware twister wasn’t yet available. A tornadic waterspout also was sighted on the Delaware River near Penns Grove, Salem County . 
 But the twisters arguably were upstaged by rare hailstorms that featured golf-ball size icy rocks, mined from frigid regions 35,000 feet in the atmosphere, that literally was plowable in some areas.
 “That was wild,” said Lee Robertson, a lead meteorologist at the weather service office in Mount Holly, who said he had witnessed nothing quite like it in his 21 years with the agency.
 Robertson, who lives in Churchville, Bucks County , was getting live reports from his 7-year-old son, Jack, who said the hailstones sounded “like jackhammers.”
 “That was something we usually see in the West and in the Plains,” said Bill Deger, senior meteorologist at AccuWeather Inc. 
 And rarely does the Philly area see tornadoes in November. It’s happened only one other time in Delaware in records dating to 1950, said Kevin Brinson, Delaware state climatologist. In fact, on average, the region experiences thunderstorms in November only once every two years.
 The Delaware tornado touched down in the vicinity of Christiana Hospital, damaging at least one helicopter, according to the weather’s service’s preliminary report.
 New Jersey hasn’t had a confirmed sighting this late in November since 1989, said Deger.
 Thursday’s tornado damaged three structures, including the Meadow View Junior Academy private school, said Burlington County spokesperson Dave Levinsky. It also caused some tree damage, the weather service noted.
 The storm struck the region with ferocity starting around 1 p.m., with the worst over by the evening commute. In addition to the twisters and the hailstones, downpours flooded numerous road throughout the region.
 No injuries or deaths were reported. 
 “It took like the perfect track to impact the most people,” said Deger, the worst of it running along the I-95 spine.
 As for the plowable hailstones that were notable in Delaware and Gloucester Counties, Deger said those hefty accumulations likely occurred near the bottoms of road valleys after all those ice marbles had rolled downhill.
 “That’s not to diminish what happened there,” he said. 
 The potential spell of riot didn’t become evident until Thursday morning when the federal Storm Prediction Center posted a discussion warning that the atmosphere over the Philly region was about to become especially volatile. 
 The storm generated powerful updrafts into frigid regions of the upper atmosphere that turned the water to ice, heavy enough to survive trips to the surface where temperatures were around 60 degrees.
 You may have noticed the dynamical storm was a prelude to quite a change in the region’s temperature fortunes.
 Highs are unlikely to get out of the 40s the next two days, and freeze warnings were in effect for the region, save for the Philly heat island and the freeze-proof Philadelphia International Airport . Freezes outside the city are likely the next several mornings.
 Come Saturday morning, it’s all but certain that some of the residual standing water will have turned to ice. 
 Given what happened Thursday, would anyone notice?
 Staff writer Lacey Latch contributed to this article.
